properties.label: D1
properties.detrimental: High bonded debt - lack of restrictions - unpaved streets.
properties.favorable: Utilities - adequate transportation to Denver - schools - nearby Fitzsimons Hospital (Army) which helps the rent situation.
properties.remarks: Area is the heart of Aurora, an incorporated town. Colfax Ave., in the center of area is dividing line between Arapahoe County on the south and Adams County on the north. Property in the Adams County section is heavily burdened with bonded debt for improvements, which is detrimental to property therein. Area is semi-agrarian and rural, occupied by gardeners and wage earners chiefly. Property is poorly kept, with unpaved streets except Colfax. There is very little sales demand but is good rent section because Fitzsimons Hospital (Army) is located in Aurora and is convenient to out of town visitors who come to be near kin folk confined to the Hospital. Mortgage lenders prefer to avoid this area except on a very conservative basis.

properties.label: C1
properties.favorable: Adequate transportation, schools, utilities.
properties.remarks: An area of small frame cottages occupied by a substantial class of low income wage earners, the kind who live within their incomes, even though small. These small houses sell readily from 1500 to 2500, terms of 10% down. Real estate men look for the area to improve and possibly build up with this type of small houses, with the establishment of the Army Air Corps Technical School to the south. It is expected that the lower income employees of the school, such as enlisted men, mechanics, will move to this area. Fitzsimons General Hospital (army) in nearby Aurora, has helped make this a good rent area.

properties.label: B4
properties.favorable: Nearby park- nearby Army Flying School (calculated to stimulate sales and rents) all utilities, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: Very spotty, difficult to analyze. Before 1900 Count Richthoffen of Germany built a castle in what is now Richthoffen Place. Few country estates went up in the neighborhood. Some well-to-do health seekers located in area. Did not built rapidly but during last few years there has been a small amount of new construction of good bungalows costing up to $8000. New Amy Air Corps Tech. School to the southeast will undoubtedly bring about the construction of a large number of bungalows in the $6000-8000 class to house officers and higher income attaches of the field. A wide variety of houses in age, style and type, it is a good ""B"" because of the class of property which predominates.

properties.label: A1
properties.favorable: Adequate schools- transportation - utilities. Nearby City Park, attractive 17th Ave. Parkway, Monaco Blvd. and Montview Blvd. in area
properties.remarks: This is the newer part of the choice Park Hill section. 17th Ave. Parkway in the area is one of the very attractive boulevards of the city. Monaco Blvd. and Montview Blvd. in the area are two other boulevards artistically landscaped, and built up on both sides with the better class of homes. Although some of the houses on East 17th Ave. Parkway and Montview Blvd. are 20-25 years old, they maintain their character of exclusiveness and desirability. The fact that the area is ""Park Hill"" adds to its desirability.

properties.label: B1
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation- schools- churches.
properties.remarks: This outer fringe of the Park Hill section is newer than B-2. The vacant ground to the north and cast offers unlimited opportunity for future building. The area has built slowly away from the heart of the Park Hill section (B-2) and naturally houses near B-2 are older. The area is occupied by a moderate income group- white collar people, clerks and small business men. A good ""B"" lacking the ""tone and exclusiveness"" of A-1 and A-2. An appreciable amount of new construction would make the outer fringe an ""A"". It is not too spotty to class first grade, but it is a very good ""B"".

properties.label: B2
properties.favorable: Adjoining Cheesman Park and Golf Course- good schools in area- churches - good transportation - all utilities.
properties.remarks: The heart of Park Hill section, long considered one of the most desirable in Denver, the ""elite"" section for many years. Although it is built up with some houses 25 years old, it continues to hold its desirability, chiefly because of schools, proximity to City Park and partly because it is ""Park Hill."" Older house are usually well reconditioned. 17th Parkway is a wide thoroughfare, beautifully kept, but houses between Colorado Blvd. and Dexter are too old to be graded ""A"". A good sales demand prevails. It is a very good rent district. Still considered the best residential section of Denver by many ""moderate income"" business and professional people. A good B area.

properties.label: B3
properties.detrimental: Schools are across two heavy traffic highways (Colfax and Colorado Blvd.) for those residing south of Colfax.
properties.favorable: Adequate transportation- all utilities
properties.remarks: A sooty section with newer houses south of Colfax bordering A-2. The security between Batavia and Colfax is older and inferior. Colfax Ave. east of Colorado Blvd. is dotted with business houses. A fair demand for houses exists but buyers much prefer to select houses in older adjoining B-2. One reason is the school situation. A fair ""B"".

properties.label: A2
properties.favorable: Adequate transportation- utilities- churches. Community Center on Colfax.
properties.remarks: An attractive bungalow area, virtually all of which has been built since 1929. Houses are uniform in style, size and quality. The vacant area to the east and south will undoubtedly build up with a substantial type of brick bungalow. While this area does not rank with A-1, 3, 4, and 5 in the size or cost of homes, it stands out as the best moderately-price new section of Denver.

properties.label: C2
properties.favorable: Nearby Golf Course and City Park- adequate transportation- all utilities.
properties.remarks: 30 new houses of the $4000-4800 class were built on Milwaukee and Fillmore between 29th and 33rd during the first half of 1938. Were largely FHA financed and bought by wage earners with small down payments. Area is spotty with many older houses. Better paid wage earners from nearby industrial plants occupy it and help make sales and rent situation favorable. Bordering the Golf Course between St. Paul and Colorado Blvd. are large new expensive structures, but this better section is too small to classify separately. As a whole is a good working mans' area, where there is likely to be more new building of cheaper type.

properties.label: D12
properties.detrimental: Negro and foreign infiltration- commercial encroachments.
properties.favorable: Utilities- adequate transportation - schools.
properties.remarks: This section, bordering the heavy commercial district to the west and northwest, is an old area now occupied by a combination of Negroes, Mexicans and a transient class of workers. The west and northwest part of it is Denver's closest approach to a slum district. Shacks, largely held by speculators, rent for as low as $5 per month. Negroes occupy the eastern and better part of the area. Cheap houses in the area have a good rental demand. A poor 4th grade section.

properties.label: D13
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation- schools- churches.
properties.remarks: This is a better Negro section of Denver and is one of the best colored districts in the United States. The northeastern part of it is often referred to as the ""Negro Country Club"". It is an old brick section with a reasonably large number of well-kept newer houses, mostly occupied by Negroes. It is not a typical Negro area of cheap, tumble-down ill-kept shacks found in eastern and mid-western cities, but all of the colored occupants are housed in brick structures- either detached or in terraces. For a Negro section it is very well kept up. Were it not for the heavy colored population much of it could be rated ""C"". In financing home ownership, the better class negroes usually obtain loans from institutions; but others are victims of industrial operators who have high fees and high interest rates.

properties.label: C6
properties.favorable: Schools, utilities, adequate transportation; churches, close in.
properties.remarks: Forty to 50 yrs. ago this was in the swank ""Capitol Hill"" areas, occupied by Denver's leading families. The mansions of that day have turned to clubs, rooming houses and made-over apartments, to a greater extent than any other area of Denver. Being close-in it is perfectly suited to this type of usage. The large old homes are also being turned to business houses. It is also an apartment district. A good substantial class of clerks and office people live in the rooming houses and apartments. The area, turning commercial, should display good ground values in the future.

properties.label: C5
properties.favorable: East High School in area, City Park, Business houses on East Colfax- Schools- all utilities, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: An area of 2-story houses for which there is now no active demand. The better part of the area is that east of Monroe, where the security is newer. The area is occupied by a large number of original owners of houses ranging in age from 25 years up, and is beginning to witness transition to rooming houses in the west end; also some commercial encroachments other than those near Colfax, which is a business street. A typical the good 3rd grade section which is due to decline in the future because of the age of the properties.

properties.label: B5
properties.favorable: Nearby 7th Ave. Parkway- all utilities- adequate transportation- good schools.
properties.remarks: This is a high assessment section. The houses within a block of the boundaries of A-4 are high grade, well kept structures bordering on first grade Nearer 10th Ave. they are older. The area as a whole enjoys a favorable reflex from particularly 7th Ave. and its attractive parkway. Were it not that the sections nearest 7th Ave. are entirely built up and above 10 years old, they could properly be classed first grade. A very good second grade area which will retain its character for several years.

properties.label: A4
properties.favorable: Beautifully landscaped parkway in center of wide street, all utilities, adequate transportation, schools, churches, nearby Cheesman Park.
properties.remarks: Although 7th Ave. Parkway almost entirely built up, with some houses 15 yrs old, it would be odd to visualize the city without this section, classed A or among the very best. With 7th Ave. Parkway and beautifully kept yards, it is indeed an outstanding section of better class homes, housing some of Denver's wealthiest, most affluent citizens. Strangely, the cemetery abutting 3 1/2 blocks between Cheesman Park and York, has made no difference to the desirability of the adjoining section. There is an exclusiveness about the area that helps to sustain values. It will hold its character for several years. Many of Denver's finest homes are in this area. Lenders advised that the security herein is acceptable for as high a ratio and as long in periods as new A-3 and A-6.

properties.label: A3
properties.detrimental: None outstanding except the uncertain influence of the nearby Army Air Corps Technical School.
properties.favorable: Trend in better home construction definitely to this area, with much vacant ground north and south for expansion -restricted- utilities and adequate transportation. Park in the southwest part of area- school facilities.
properties.remarks: Denver's most intense activity in construction of the better type of houses is centered in this area. Crestmoor Addition (east of Holly, south of 6th) developed by Garrett-Bromfield, is a well planned sub-division wherein newly built houses are selling for $10, 500 to 29,000. The section surrounding Mountain View Park is being built up with substantial structures running from $7000 to $15,000. The lower priced houses (as low as $5500) are being put up north of 6th between Colorado Blvd. and Fairfax. It is a new area entirely, and Crestmoor is Denver's newest high priced subdivision. A house recently sold to Jew in Crestmoor brought summary action in barring the builder from future work in the area. The undeveloped land to the south offers great possibilities of future development. Since the area was begun, three to four years ago, the Army Air Corps Technical School has been located a short distance to the southeast. The extent to which this will be detrimental to the exclusive area cannot yet be estimated. The trend is definitely to this area, including the undeveloped sections on the north and south of it. The new development in the southwest part of this area began in full view and knowledge of the poor houses in C-9 and D-2. A-3 is on higher ground than D-2 and C-9 and Colorado Blvd. which divides them, is a wide thoroughfare, something of a natural barrier. With respect to adjoining D-2 and C-9, it can only be said that high priced houses are being built and sold in the southwest part of A-3.

properties.label: D2
properties.detrimental: Dumping grounds north of Cherry Creek.
properties.favorable: Utilities - adequate transportation - schools.
properties.remarks: This is a very trashy part of Harman, once a separate village. All of the houses border on shacks, streets are unpaved, and the entire southern part of the area is being used as dumping grounds to fill in along Cherry Creek. Area is lower in elevation than A-3 to the east. A-3 and A-5 were both developed with the full knowledge of this cheap area. Developers and real estate men have looked forward to buying up cheap houses in this area for newer development, should the trend to the northeastern part of Denver be sufficiently strong to warrant it. A cheap and poor section.

properties.label: C9
properties.favorable: Utilities, school, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: All of this area and portions of the adjoining area north and south was once in the village of Harman. It is very spotty with some good bungalows and other old houses of varying size and type. There are a number of Negroes in area, mostly home owners. Efforts to dislodge them have failed because they've lived there many years. A-3 on the east and A-5 on the west were both developed with full knowledge of the conditions existing in C-9. D-2 on the south is a very trashy section. This area has rather an odd relationship to A-3 and A-5, which appears not to affect the 1st grade sections. While spotty, the cheaper and older security predominates and it could be considered at best only a ""fair to poor"" 3rd grade area.

properties.label: A5
properties.detrimental: Adjoining C and D areas on the east, and several Negro families on 3rd Ave. west of York.
properties.favorable: An exclusiveness which helps sustain values, all utilities, restrictions, good transportation. County Club on south.
properties.remarks: South of 4th in this area is the exclusive Country Club. The older part of the Country Club is that west of High. Although some of the structures are 25 years old, the area seems to maintain its character, being a concentration of the social elect. North of 4th and east of High is the exclusive Park Lane Square district created 10 years ago by purchase and demolition of cheap houses, some of which were occupied by Negroes. In the heart of this Addition is the half million dollar palatial home of Mrs. Verner Z. Reed. It was the plan to join this area with Country Club to the south, but the economic depression

properties.label: B6
properties.detrimental: Inferior C-9 to the south with some Negroes.
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation- schools.
properties.remarks: An area of small brick bungalows, serving something as a buffer between the better B-5 and the spotty C-9 on the south. There is a possibility that the type of houses in this area will crowd into C-9. The area is occupied by a modest income group. Real estate men expect a continued demand for the type of property therein. A ""fair B"".

properties.label: B7
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation- schools- churches- Chessman Park
properties.remarks: Except for the small portion of this area south of 4th, it is a district of large 2-story houses; considered an exclusive section 20 to 25 years ago when it  was occupied by Denver's leading citizens. The area is attractive with its large shade trees and well maintained yards, and houses. Because of a certain exclusiveness that attaches to the area it would be too harsh to call it a ""C"", but because of the age and style of the houses it is bound to decline. This is evidenced by the poor sales demand.

properties.label: C8
properties.favorable: Close in- all utilities- churches, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: An apartment house areas, serving somewhat as a buffer between the commercial area and the better C-7. Close in, it was the ideal section for the building of apartments, 15 to 20 years ago when it had begun to decline as a residential district. Is the western ""base"" of the Capitol Hill section. Its large, old houses were once among the best in Denver; new rooming houses. As in C-7 these have declined precipitously in value in 1929. Three or four new apartments have been built in the area in the last two years. The trend will be to more apartments. A very good rent area.

properties.label: C12
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation, schools, parks, close to South Broadway industrial and commercial plants.
properties.remarks: Another wage earners' section with houses a little inferior in quality to those of C-10 and C-11. The area is spotty. In the south end east of Broadway are large old 2-story houses. Some small houses and a few terrace apts. were built in the center of the area in 1937, all designed for low income occupants. Newer houses sell for $4,000, older ones up to $3250. Railroad tracks at northern boundary are being replaced with a boulevard. Near the city limits in the southern part of the area are a number of gardens, small farms. A ""fair to average C"".

properties.label: C10
properties.favorable: Close in, with Broadway retail district in the area- All utilities, adequate transportation, schools.
properties.remarks: The reasonably large south Broadway business district, the Ford Plant, and its proximity to the downtown section, contributed to make this a very good rental section. It is a wage earners' district entirely. East of Broadway small 4 and 5 room houses predominate. The section west of Broadway is older than that cast of Broadway, bordering no a ""D"" grade. A spotty district, it is a fair ""C"".

properties.label: C11
properties.favorable: Schools- Utilities- Adequate transportation. Proximity to Washington Park.
properties.remarks: Farther removed from Broadway with its business, industrial and heavy traffic, and close to Washington Park, this area is more desirable than C-10. Houses are larger, more substantial and uniformly better in every way. The better houses are on the eastern fringe. The area has a much better grade of 2-family structures than C-10. Occupied by persons in a wide variety of occupations- small income, business and professional, clerks, mail carriers, barbers, etc., it is a good ""C'.

properties.label: C13
properties.detrimental: Lacking street improvements in part of area.
properties.favorable: Nearby Denver University- all utilities, schools, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: An area where small frame houses predominate, this being out of the zone restricted to fire proof houses. Occupied by a substantial class of clerks, wage earners and the like, the appearance of yards indicates pride of ownership. Close to Denver University, it is a choice rent section, also a good one for sales. Were the houses generally larger and more substantial this would rate a ""B"" grade. Some of the streets are unpaved but will soon be oiled. The sparsely built up portion on the south will build up with small houses. The three square blocks between Vassar and Yale, Downing to Humboldt, have built up during the last 12 months, with frames selling at from $4200 to $4900. Construction was financed by Empire Savings Building & Loan Assn. but when sold virtually all are financed through FHA loans. This type of cottages will very likely be built in greater numbers, depending on the market.

properties.label: D3
properties.detrimental: Lack of improvements - R. R. tracks.
properties.favorable: Utilities - school - fair transportation - Overland Park (golf course).
properties.remarks: Another area of cheap houses, a mixture of brick and frame, occupied by low income wage earners. Railroad tracks, the low river bed and the fact that Santa Fe Drive is a thru highway, are detrimental factors. It is in that part of Denver which failed to arouse the interest of home owners many years ago. There has been fair sales activity recently between Delaware and Broadway. The low prices of the houses are a factor with this group. Santa Fe Drive is dotted with tourist cabin parks.

properties.label: B8
properties.favorable: Washington Park, South High School, nearby Denver University, Grade Schools, adequate transportation- all utilities.
properties.remarks: This large area is very spotty, with a wide variety of houses. The 4 blocks south of Kentucky, fringing on Washington Park, too small to grade separately, is built up with very high grade structures valued up to $18,000. That portion to the north, adjoining Country Club, is similar in character to parts of A-5, but is built up and will decline because of age. It is a brick bungalow area with some cottages in the southeast portion. Washington Park and South High School, as well as nearby Denver University, are distinctly favorable influences. This should be a good area for years to come. It is the heart of section referred to as ""South Denver"" where values held up reasonably well.

properties.label: A6
properties.favorable: Suburban atmosphere with much room for expansion- highly restricted - all utilities - good transportation.
properties.remarks: This is Bonnie Brae, opened for development 10-12 years ago. The sub-division heavily bonded for improvements when the economic set back, following 1929, arrested expansion temporarily. Many lots were sold for taxes. The area was recently (spring of 1938) involved in some scandal wherein a city official was found to be acquiring and selling lots from information obtained on the inside but this did not injure the area from the standpoint of desirability. Bondholders committees are selling lots. Area appears due for immediate development in houses built for $9000 and under. East of Steele and north of Kentucky is the estate and mansion of Ex-U.S Senator L.C Phipps, Pennsylvania-born multi-millionaire. His house cost $500,000 a few years ago.

properties.label: C14
properties.favorable: Denver University on south- grade schools- all utilities- adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: A spotty area indeed. There are too many large old houses, built when this was very much suburban, to grade this area ""B"" but it is, as a whole, a good ""C"". There are a number of new houses, costing up to $9000, in the area. Denver University on the south is favorable to the section, several school officers having built good houses therein. Some of the older houses have turned to boarding houses. The school makes it an excellent rent district. Fraternity houses in the area do not help it, and other aspects of school activity are detrimental to a small degree.

properties.label: B9
properties.favorable: Washington Park- Schools - adequate transportation-all utilities.
properties.remarks: The fact that this area borders on Washington Park, with a substantial type of good bungalows, sets it out from the surrounding 3rd grade section. There is a definite break between Corona and Ogden, in the type of houses. The Park is the principal reason why this area has maintained its character. A fair ""B"" section.

properties.label: D16
properties.detrimental: Stench from packing plants- lack of improvements.
properties.favorable: Utilities- adequate transportation- fair school facilities.
properties.remarks: The security in this area is cheaper than that in nearby D-15. The area is occupied entirely by workers from the packing plants, stockyards and railroad shops. On the northern edge of the city this section is little known to real estate men who pay little or no attention to it. The only demand for property is by low income wage earners who do not mind the stench from the stockyards area. Streets are unpaved. In an undeveloped area part of the city, between R.R. tracks, with its small, poorly built houses, the area is a ""fair to poor D"" typical of any such section near a meat packing industry,

properties.label: D5
properties.favorable: Utilities - adequate transportation - school.
properties.remarks: This is the Valverde district which failed many years ago to develop into anything but a section of workingman's houses. That portion fronting on Alameda is an attractive street of well-kept small stucco houses, easily better than a 4th grade. But off Alameda to the south the terrain is hilly, streets unpaved, houses are a variety of small cheap frames. For some reason the area has not displayed the sales demand of D-8, although more attractive. The fact that Alameda is a heavy-traffic thoroughfare offsets to some extent the nicer homes on that street. The area has a high percentage of home ownership because it meets the demand for a certain type of house which wage earners can afford. A good 4th grade section.

properties.label: D11
properties.remarks: A few blocks of shacks in this small area, located in the R.R yards, are inhabited by the lowest type of laborers. Some of them are section hands for the railroads. Property herein has virtually no sales value, and no broker would bother with the area. No house therein would sell for more than $300.

properties.label: D15
properties.detrimental: Unpaved streets- stench from stockyards and packing plants west of the area.
properties.favorable: Adequate transportation- schools, utilities.
properties.remarks: An area occupied entirely by industrial workers from the packing plants, stockyards to the west and other plants nearby. It has a wide range and variety of houses from cheap frames to some fair bungalows. Many are ill kept, with outside toilets. Real estate men pay little attention to the area. Demand for homes is entirely by wage earners of the low income brackets, who do not mind the stench from the stockyards districts. A fair ""D"".

properties.label: D14
properties.detrimental: Mixture of foreigners and negroes - lack of improvements. Stench from packing plants.
properties.favorable: Stores- schools- churches- adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: This is Globeville, a small rural section of the cheap houses occupied entirely by wage earners from nearby R.R shops, packing plants and stock yards. The majority are foreign born or of South European descent. Hungarians, Poles, and Bulgarians predominate. This section has a reasonably high degree of home ownership for this type of an old cheap section, due to the high regard of foreigners for home ownership . As long as there is a demand for the type of small low-cost houses, found in this section, on the part of industrial workers, sales will be good, especially with small down payments. A good 4th grade section.

properties.label: D6
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation, schools, churches.
properties.remarks: In this old area, flanked by commercial and industrial sections, are many small, cheap terraces containing approximately 1,000 living units. There are also 200, 2-family structures and about 900 ""doubles"" in the area. It is old and has deteriorated to a typical residential area bordering heavy commercial and industrial districts. In the northwest part of the area, and bordering the industrial district to the west, is a Mexican concentration. There are the usual large number of industrial and commercial encroachments in all parts of the area. Because of its proximity to railroad yards and shops, this area has always been occupied by railroad workers principally. Structures near the railroad yards are cheap, having deteriorated considerably since 1929. Some of these ramshackle terraces have been picked up by speculators. It is a good rent area. Sales have been slow. Speculators have been reasonably active in this area for many years.

properties.label: D7
properties.favorable: See item 5 below
properties.remarks: This area is an area of scattered old shacks and brick houses, ranking with D-11 and the northwestern part of D-12 as the very poorest part of Denver. Ground from Federal Blvd. to the river hed is very rugged and unattractive. It is occupied by a poor class of laborers and virtually all occupants of the area are on some type of relief. Mexicans live in the northern part of it, bordering the industrial section. A very cheap and poor area indeed. It is known as ""Frog Hollow"".

properties.label: D8
properties.detrimental: High assessment for improvements- unpaved streets.
properties.favorable: A continuing demand by low income wage earners, schools, churches, adequate transportation- utilities.
properties.remarks: Practically everything south of 10th is known as Barnum, named after P. T Barnum, circus tycoon, who was induced by a real estate enthusiast to buy virtually the whole section many years ago. He discovered that the area lacked water and the trend would not be in that direction, so after wintering his circus here for several years, traded off the land. It is a hilly section, unattractive and occupied by a variety of cheap frame houses, some shacks and some fairly good wage earners' homes. It is a heavy special assessment section, which is detrimental to the property therein. It is a good sale section, answering the need of low income wage earners for shelter without many of the amenities. A few cheap cottages have been constructed during the last year. That portion north of 13th is occupied by a poor class of Jews, and is a terrace district. Considered as a whole, this is a good 4th grade section because it meets the needs of a low income class, but it is a ragged and a spotty district.

properties.label: C16
properties.detrimental: Preponderance of Jews, restricting market to this class.
properties.favorable: Business district - schools - churches (Jewish) - adequate transportation - all utilities.
properties.remarks: The poorer Jewish section of West Denver. A spotty area with a wide variety of houses from shacks to reasonably good brick bungalows. There are a few apartments and terraces in the area, all Jewish-occupied. The lower class Jews live in this and the adjoining northern portion of D-8. The market is limited to Jewish buyers who usually are able to buy below the market value, a condition prevailing in B-10, the better Jewish section. West Colfax is dotted with business houses, all Jewish owned and operated. A poor third grade section.

properties.label: B10
properties.favorable: Nearby business district, schools, churches (Jewish) and adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: A 100% Jewish district, much better than the surrounding ""C"" area, also Jewish. Houses are well-kept brick bungalows, uniform in size. Is occupied by a reasonably good class of moderate income Jews, including business and professional men. Those who become affluent usually move to better parts of the city. Although mortgage money is readily available, many lenders, including insurance companies, stay out of the area. Sales are usually at prices below the market because of the Jewish trait of bargaining. It is graded ""B"" because of substantial type of houses and good appearance of the section. Is a good section as long as it is entirely Jewish. Is no demand (sales or rental) by non-Jewish occupants. Some of the leading brokers will not handle property herein. West Colfax from Federal Blvd. to the city limits is dotted with Jewish business houses.

properties.label: C17
properties.detrimental: Lack of improvements - lack of restrictions.
properties.favorable: Utilities - transportation to city limits (Sheridan) - schools - churches.
properties.remarks: There has been a fair demand for property recently in this area which is Edgewater, outside the city limits. In the sparsely built up portion between 29th and 32nd there has been considerable building of houses costing as high as $5500 during the last 2 years. Between 26th and 20th the area is very spotty, running from large 2-story houses in good repair, to small frames on the southern fringe. It is a wage earner's area. It has all utilities including water purchased from the city of Denver. Street car transportation ends at Sheridan. A ""fair C"".

properties.label: B11
properties.favorable: All utilities- good transportation-- school -- churches.
properties.occupation: Moderate income business, clerks, wage earners
properties.remarks: A spotty area of reasonably new construction surrounded by C-18 with its variety of houses, some as old as 40 years. It is, like B-12, located on the highest elevation in Denver. The newly built houses, attractive brick bungalows are selling for as high as $6,000. The area is like all of North Denver- built up at random, new houses among the old, but the better type of buildings predominate. The elevation and view of the mountains to the west are favorable factors. A ""reasonably good B"".

properties.label: C18
properties.favorable: All utilities - adequate transportation - schools, including new junior high at W. 21 and Perry.
properties.occupation: Clerks, wage earners, moderate income business
properties.remarks: A good ""average"" section which helps sustain values in the North Denver area. It is spotty with large variety of structures in age and type, some as old as 40-45 years. There are also new brick bungalows scattered through the area. A new Junior High School at West 21st and Perry will undoubtedly build up that sparsely built up section east of Sloan's Lake. Area is the best 3rd grade section in North Denver, being superior in type and quality of houses to C-17,19, 20. Because of age of most of the houses it can only be graded as ""C""-one of the very best 3rd grade sections of Denver. Occupied by a wide variety of moderate income people, it will be a good area for some time to come for this type of occupants. A ""good C"".

properties.label: D9
properties.detrimental: Location on hill, sloping toward R.R yards.
properties.favorable: Schools- adequate transportation - all utilities.
properties.remarks: Virtually this entire area is located on a hill ascending from the lower river bed to Federal Blvd. on the west and 32nd Street on the north. It is the oldest section of North Denver, occupied entirely by wage earners and laborers of the lower income class, a large percentage of which are on relief. There is a variety of 2-family and multi-family structures in area. It is one of the older and cheaper sections of Denver, with no demand for property. There is a good rental demand in the cheaper class of houses.

properties.label: D10
properties.favorable: Utilities- churches (Italian Catholic) -adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: The poorer Italians are concentrated in this area, which is an old cheap section. There is no demand for property. The sparsely built up part of the area to the north is one of the small farms and gardens. A poor fourth grade section.

properties.label: C19
properties.favorable: Schools - adequate transportation - all utilities.
properties.remarks: A truly spotty area with a wide variety of houses, some good brick bungalows and many old, poor ones. The four or five blocks in the east end of the area is debatable territory between a ""C"" and ""D"". Nearer Federal Blvd. are some good brick, 5 and 6 room structures. North of 44th, not more than 30% built up, are 12 or 15 new brick bungalows in the $5500 class. The area is Italian dominated. During prohibition days, the illicit liquor traffic centered here. Repeal and consequent destruction of bootlegging, affected residential values, particularly the better houses which had been built by prosperous Italian bootleggers. The ambition of the Italians in this area is to move up with the higher class Italians in B-12. The area is 50% Italian including these of the 2nd and 3rd generation.

properties.label: C20
properties.detrimental: Elitch's Gardens and Lakeside Park adjoining on south and west, respectively, both amusement parks.
properties.favorable: Near Regis College and Berkeley Park, all utilities - adequate transportation - schools.
properties.remarks: Section of small frame houses quite similar in character to those in C-1 and C-15. Is a cheaper section of North Denver, housing wage earners and small income people. 3 parks with lakes, help the area considerably. It is a good sales area because of demand for cheaper houses, and by the same token, a good rent area. That portion west of Sheridan is in Edgewater, outside the city limits, but the type of houses is the same as in other parts of area, and is very little difference in other matters affecting home ownership outside the city. This should be a good workingman's section for many years. A ""fair C"".

properties.label: C15
properties.detrimental: Lack of restriction or zoning ordinance- many unpaved streets, no sewer in sparesly built portions.
properties.favorable: Adequate schools, good transportation to Denver- all utilities, except sewer in sparsely built southeast portion, good business section.
properties.remarks: This is the better part of Englewood (Pop. 9,000) adjoining Denver on the south. The city is one of small cottages (95% frame) occupied by modest income wage earners, the great majority of whom are employed in Denver. This area is very spotty. That portion north of Hampden is made up of small frames, two to five room houses, except the northwest portion where there are some good, brick houses. On South Sherman, from Jefferson to Mansfield, are the best homes in the city- a solid block of good bricks and another block of new frame structures. A drawback to the section is lack of restrictions, but city officials contemplate enactment of a zoning ordinance soon. The area is only ""fair to poor"" C, due to the large variety of houses, most of them small and cheaply constructed; unpaved streets, lack of restrictions.

properties.label: D4
properties.detrimental: Lack of restrictions or zoning ordinance - unpaved streets - R. R. at west - encroachment of Negroes near R. R. tracks.
properties.favorable: Adequate transportation to Denver - schools - churches - business center.
properties.remarks: This is the older and poorer part of Englewood. A number of Negro families have moved in to the section between Oxford and Hampden near the R. R. tracks. That section north and east of the Eaglewood High School is in a draw, which is distinctly detrimental. Influences which apply to C-15 also affect D-4, but in the latter area the security is much inferior.

properties.label: C7
properties.favorable: Schools, churches. All utilities, adequate transportation.
properties.remarks: This is the Capitol Hill section, 25 years ago the ""Gold Coast"" of Denver. It has suffered a terrific shrinkage in values since 1929 as large, expensive houses, 20 to 40 years old, go begging on the market. An inspection of sales cards in the office of Van Schaak & Company, disclosed that houses offered at about $100,000 in 1919 were quoted at $65,000 to $75,000 in 1929 and today can be had for around $15,000. The less expensive of the fine old houses have dropped from 50% to 70% in value since 1929. Many of Denver's leading

properties.label: C3
properties.favorable: All utilities- adequate transportation- schools, nearby City Park.
properties.remarks: An older area than C-2, some of the houses being 50 years old. However, the property is pretty well preserved. Negroes are crowding the area from the west, although deed restrictions bar them from C-30. Industrial workers from the plants to the north occupy the area. It is a ""fair"" or ""average"" third grade section.
